title: Lock The Default, Own The Front Door
documentTitle: Samsung RSA 2020 Term Sheet — Deal 1 (Email from Anna Kartasheva to Jim Kolotouros)
excerptForBlog: With the exception of Bixby (and/or successors): Edit based on product direction of Search/Assistant. We should add that Search within Google Assistant must default to Google and they can't promote/suggest that End Users change that. All other search access points (Launchers, Keyboards, Bixby, etc.): Google shall be the default for all search access points and Samsung shall receive revenue share for all designated and future search access points implemented prior to or during the course of the Contemplated Agreement. Suggestion: Add 'anywhere on a Core Qualified Device.'

lessonTitle: Lock The Default, Own The Front Door
pullQuote: When you can't win the device, win every doorway on it.
leadershipTraits: writes contracts for the future, not the present
situation: In June 2020, Google's Anna Kartasheva emailed Jim Kolotouros with proposed language for a revenue-sharing deal with Samsung. The document is a term sheet negotiation. The core issue: which search engine is the default across every entry point on Samsung devices — launchers, keyboards, and beyond.
insight: The document's language is surgical. It doesn't just ask for default status on the main search bar. It targets 'all search access points' and even proposes adding the phrase 'anywhere on a Core Qualified Device.' That's a platform lockout move — closing every gap before a competitor can squeeze through one. The one explicit carve-out is Bixby, Samsung's own assistant, which signals Google understood when to stop pushing. The revenue share offer is the lever that makes Samsung willing to accept these constraints. Google trades money for exclusivity across the full device surface. That's **switching costs** engineered at the contract level, not the product level — before a user ever opens the phone.
application: If you're negotiating a distribution or partnership deal, map every access point your product could occupy — then negotiate for all of them, not just the obvious one. Offer your partner something real (revenue, traffic, data) in exchange. The gap you leave unaddressed today is the gap a competitor will walk through tomorrow.
